claims.text: The target material is a quaternary equiatomic FCC alloy.
The target alloy has a homogeneous microstructure and a high initial dislocation density.
A vacuum-induction-melted and annealed CoCrFeNiMn alloy provides a relevant analogue for the target quaternary alloy.
The target alloy's yield strength will become relatively insensitive to strain rate at 500–600 °C.
At 500–600 °C, the deformation mechanism transitions from dislocation glide to stress-assisted dislocation climb.
The activation barrier for climb becomes rate-limiting rather than dislocation mobility.
Stress-assisted dislocation climb is controlled by lattice diffusion.
Dynamically formed M23C6 carbides or Cr-rich sigma phase may obstruct dislocations.
Thermal activation at intermediate temperature enables dislocations to climb over precipitates or forest dislocations.
The high-stress-region stress exponent will be between 8.9 and 14.
The high-stress-region activation energy will be approximately 380 kJ/mol.
A high stress exponent and activation energy indicate a shift from glide to diffusion-limited climb.
Diffusion-limited climb produces a plateau or minimal variation of yield strength with strain rate.
At room or lower temperatures, dislocation glide produces strong yield-strength dependence on strain rate, with n approximately 3–5 and lower activation energy.
Below 500 °C, glide dominates and strain-rate sensitivity is high.
Above 600 °C, dynamic recrystallization and grain-boundary sliding introduce new strain-rate dependencies.
The glide-to-climb transition temperature and activation energy depend on alloy composition, solute drag, and precipitate type.
Tangled dislocation networks observed by TEM signify glide, whereas dislocation loops or voids signify climb.
Values of n below 6 and activation energy below 270 kJ/mol at 550 °C would demonstrate continued glide domination and high strain-rate sensitivity.

contradictions.description: The cited stress-exponent values use the conventional creep relation in which n is the slope of log(strain rate) versus log(stress), but the proposed measurement defines n as the inverse slope, log(stress) versus log(strain rate). That procedure would yield approximately 1/n rather than values of 8.9–14.

The design specifies constant applied stress of 300 MPa while also prescribing two distinct strain rates. In a conventional constant-stress creep test, strain rate is an observed response rather than an independently imposed variable, so the loading protocol is internally underspecified.
